sections.title: How a solar farm actually gets built
ps: The build sequence is a moving assembly line across thousands of acres: survey and grade → drive steel piles (thousands of them, GPS-guided) → bolt on tracker rows (motorized racking that follows the sun) → clamp on modules → pull DC cable to combiner boxes → inverters convert DC to AC → collection system feeds the substation

It's a productivity game, not a craftsmanship game: crews are measured in piles per day and modules per hour, so weather, labor availability, and terrain surprises translate directly into margin — the same acre-by-acre repetition that makes solar cheap makes its costs brittle
Trackers changed the economics twice over: single-axis tracking adds ~15-25% more energy than fixed tilt, but adds motors, controllers, and wind-stow logic — more to install and more to maintain

The electrical balance of system (combiners, inverters, MV collection, the substation) is where solar EPC meets classic power construction — and where contractors with T&D roots have an edge over pure panel-installers

sections.title: Reading a public contractor's earnings
ps: Public companies report quarterly against analyst consensus — the averaged forecast of covering analysts. 'Beat' and 'miss' move the stock more than absolute results, because the price already embeds the expectation

Adjusted (non-GAAP) EPS strips out items management deems non-recurring (amortization from acquisitions, one-time charges); GAAP EPS is the audited legal number. A company can beat on adjusted while losing money on GAAP — always check which number a headline cites

Guidance — management's own forecast for the year — is often the real news: a company can beat the quarter and crater on a guidance cut, because guidance resets every model. Serial guidance cuts destroy credibility faster than a single bad quarter
Different data vendors (Zacks, FactSet, Bloomberg) survey different analyst sets, so 'consensus' isn't one number — borderline quarters can be a beat on one vendor's set and a miss on another's

sections.title: Backlog quality: why $13.9 billion isn't one number
ps: Backlog is signed-but-unearned work, but its quality varies enormously: MSA (master service agreement) backlog is recurring unit-price work under multi-year utility frameworks — sticky, lower-risk, re-priced regularly; fixed-price project backlog locks a price years ahead against uncertain costs

The risk profile inverts intuition: a giant fixed-price megaproject can sink a company while a thousand small MSA jobs cannot — which is why analysts read the backlog MIX (MSA vs fixed, next-12-month vs beyond) before the headline number

Backlog can hit records while earnings collapse: new awards keep flowing on demand strength even as old projects burn cost — backlog measures the future book, overruns hit the current income statement
A backlog quality checklist: who bears escalation risk, what share is fixed-price, how concentrated by customer/segment, and how much converts to revenue within 12 months

sections.title: Percentage-of-completion: how overruns hide and then explode
ps: Contractors book revenue as work progresses — typically cost-to-cost: if you've spent 40% of estimated total cost, you recognize 40% of contract revenue. The method's engine is the ESTIMATE of total cost at completion ('cost to complete')

When the estimate is wrong, the past restates itself through the present: discovering a project will cost 20% more forces an immediate cumulative catch-up charge — profit booked in earlier quarters reverses all at once in the quarter of discovery

That's why contractor blow-ups look sudden but aren't: the costs accreted for quarters while the estimate lagged; the disclosure is the moment the forecasting machinery finally admits it. Investors and courts then ask when management should have known

The controls that prevent it: independent project reviews, honest productivity tracking against the estimate, escalation clauses, and a culture where field teams report bad news early — 'project controls' is the discipline the whole edifice rests on

sections.title: Behind-the-meter gas: the fast power AI can't wait for
ps: When the grid queue runs years, a data center can generate its own power on-site: gas engines or turbines behind the meter, sometimes fully off-grid — trading fuel logistics and emissions permits for immediate, controllable megawatts

The two machine families: reciprocating engines (RICE — modular ~1-20 MW units, fast-start, tolerate load swings well, arrive quickly) and gas turbines (larger blocks, better heat rates at scale, longer lead times); AI campuses increasingly use fleets of engines as bridge power until grid interconnection arrives
An off-grid AI power plant is a microgrid: generation, switchgear, controls, and the campus load form an island that must balance itself — frequency and voltage stability with no grid to lean on

'Bridge power' shapes contracts: gear is often sized and permitted for a 3-7 year bridge, then the campus converts to grid supply and the engines become backup — the EPC gets paid for speed, not just capacity

sections.title: When contractors buy contractors: M&A logic in specialty construction
ps: Specialty contractors are valued on EBITDA multiples — a buyer paying $422M for a firm earning ~$40M of EBITDA is paying ~10x, betting the acquired capability earns more inside its platform than the multiple implies

What's really being bought is workforce and customer position: 600 electricians with data-center experience cannot be hired one-by-one in this labor market, and incumbent relationships with hyperscaler programs take years to earn
Integration risk runs through people: craft workers and project managers can walk, so buyers keep brands, leadership, and compensation intact — the asset has legs
Timing cuts both ways: debt-funded acquisitions closed at the cycle top look expensive if the buyer's own stock then halves — the balance-sheet sequencing matters as much as the strategic logic

flashcards.q: What is the physical build sequence of a utility-scale solar farm?
flashcards.a: Survey/grade → drive GPS-guided steel piles → bolt on tracker rows → clamp modules → pull DC cable to combiners → inverters convert DC to AC → medium-voltage collection feeds the substation. It runs like a moving assembly line across thousands of acres, measured in piles per day.

flashcards.q: What does single-axis tracking add to a solar plant, and at what cost?
flashcards.a: Racking that rotates panels to follow the sun adds roughly 15-25% more energy than fixed tilt — but adds motors, controllers, and wind-stow logic, meaning more installation work and more maintenance.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between GAAP and adjusted (non-GAAP) EPS?
flashcards.a: GAAP EPS is the audited legal number. Adjusted EPS strips items management deems non-recurring (acquisition amortization, one-time charges). A company can beat on adjusted while losing money on GAAP — always check which number a headline cites.

flashcards.q: Why can a company beat its quarter and still see the stock crash?
flashcards.a: Guidance. Management's forecast for the year resets every analyst model — a solid quarter paired with a guidance cut reprices the whole future. Serial guidance cuts destroy credibility faster than one bad quarter.

Different vendors (Zacks, FactSet, Bloomberg, and others) average different sets of analyst forecasts. A borderline quarter can be a beat against one vendor's consensus and a miss against another's — earnings verdicts depend on whose number you use.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between MSA backlog and fixed-price backlog?
flashcards.a: MSA backlog is recurring unit-price work under multi-year utility framework agreements — sticky, re-priced regularly, low blow-up risk. Fixed-price backlog locks a price years ahead against uncertain costs. The mix matters more than the headline total.

flashcards.q: How can backlog hit a record while earnings collapse?
flashcards.a: Backlog measures the future book (signed, unearned work); overruns hit the current income statement. New awards keep flowing on strong demand even as old projects burn cost — the two numbers describe different time periods.

flashcards.q: How does percentage-of-completion accounting recognize revenue?
flashcards.a: Proportionally to progress, usually cost-to-cost: spend 40% of the estimated total cost, recognize 40% of contract revenue. The whole method rests on the estimate of cost at completion — get that wrong and reported profit is wrong too.

flashcards.q: Why do contractor cost overruns appear 'suddenly' in one quarter?
flashcards.a: The cumulative catch-up: when the cost-to-complete estimate is revised upward, profit recognized in earlier quarters reverses all at once in the discovery quarter. Costs accreted for months while the estimate lagged — the disclosure is just the moment the forecast admits it.

flashcards.q: Why would an AI data center build its own gas power plant behind the meter?
flashcards.a: Grid interconnection queues run years; on-site generation delivers controllable megawatts immediately. Fleets of fast-start reciprocating engines often serve as 3-7 year 'bridge power' until grid supply arrives, then convert to backup.

flashcards.q: Reciprocating engines vs gas turbines for on-site power — what's the trade?
flashcards.a: Recips (RICE): modular ~1-20 MW units, fast-start, handle load swings well, short lead times — ideal for bridge power. Turbines: bigger blocks, better efficiency at scale, longer factory queues. An off-grid campus is a self-balancing microgrid either way.

flashcards.q: When a contractor pays ~10x EBITDA to acquire a specialty electrical firm, what is it really buying?
flashcards.a: Workforce and customer position: hundreds of experienced electricians who can't be hired individually in this labor market, plus incumbent relationships with hyperscaler programs. Integration risk runs through people — so buyers preserve brand, leadership, and pay to keep the asset from walking.
